passage: Meher, you heard about Anand, right? He failed the Olympiad qualifier. Honestly, I'm not even surprised. It was obvious. He played the district cricket final the Sunday before the exam. Who does that? And he only did two mock papers. Anyone could have seen this coming. What? ...Okay, yes, I said last week he'd clear it easily. But that was before. No, listen, I'm Tarun, I sit next to him, I know how he studies. ...Fine, you're right, I also told him to play the final. I said one day wouldn't matter. It didn't seem like a big deal then. The paper was just really hard this year, wasn't it? Half the school failed it. Hmm. So maybe it wasn't that obvious. Maybe it only looks obvious now. Don't tell Anand I said it was obvious, okay?

qa.q: Which match did Anand play the Sunday before the exam?
qa.a: He played the district cricket final.

qa.q: Why does it feel "obvious" to Tarun now that Anand would fail?
qa.a: Knowing the result makes the cricket match and the two mock papers look like clear warning signs, so Tarun feels confident it was predictable. Tarun's memory quietly skips the earlier belief that Anand would clear it easily.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Tarun's thinking?
qa.a: When Meher brought up Tarun's words from last week and the advice to play the final, Tarun realised the outcome had looked open before, and it only looks obvious now.

qa.q: How might Anand feel if he heard Tarun calling his failure obvious?
qa.a: Anand would likely feel hurt and blamed, especially since Tarun had encouraged him to play the final and said one day wouldn't matter.

grounding: A teenager says a friend's Olympiad failure was obvious, until reminded of expecting the opposite beforehand.

passage: I'm Sachin, Kashish's older brother, and I've been watching my sister this week. I don't know everything she's thinking, but here's what I saw. Her friend Mitali didn't get into the science stream at the new school; she missed the cut-off by three marks. At dinner Kashish said, "It was so obvious. She kept going to dance practice in exam month. Of course she didn't make it." But I remember a month ago, Kashish was the one saying, "Mitali's so smart, she'll get in without trying." When I reminded her, she frowned and said, "I didn't mean it like that." Then later, on the phone with Mitali, her voice was very soft, and she didn't mention dance at all. Maybe she noticed. Maybe she just felt bad. I'm not sure. But she stopped saying "obvious" after that.

qa.q: By how many marks did Mitali miss the cut-off?
qa.a: She missed the cut-off by three marks.

qa.q: Why might Kashish have said Mitali's failure was "so obvious"?
qa.a: Once Kashish knew the result, the dance practice looked like a clear mistake, so she felt confident saying so. Her memory seemed to rewrite her earlier belief that Mitali would get in easily.

qa.q: After Sachin's reminder, what choice did Kashish seem to make?
qa.a: She stopped using the word "obvious" and spoke softly to Mitali without blaming the dance practice, which was fairer to Mitali's choice.

qa.q: How might Mitali feel if she heard her choices called obviously wrong?
qa.a: Mitali would likely feel judged unfairly, since she chose dance when nobody, not even Kashish, expected her to miss the cut-off.

grounding: A brother observes his sister calling her friend's exam failure obvious, although she had predicted success a month before.

passage:
"So the biryani stall flopped," said Arif bhai, pouring tea. "Obviously. Who sells biryani at a fest in April heat? Everyone wanted cold drinks."
"Totally obvious," agreed Nazia, his wife, "and it was right next to the gate. Too much dust."
Shreya, twenty and still sore, put down her cup. "Wait. When we chose biryani in February, what did we know?"
"That it'd be hot?"
"The fest was supposed to be in the evening. They moved it to two p.m. three days before. And last year's biryani stall sold out."
Nazia paused. "Okay. And the gate spot?"
"That was the only spot left after the committee reshuffled. We didn't choose it."
Arif bhai scratched his beard. "Hmm. So it wasn't a stupid plan."
"It was a reasonable plan with bad luck," said Shreya. "Next time we'll ask what happens if the timing changes."

qa.q: What time did the fest get moved to?
qa.a: They moved it to two p.m. three days before.

qa.q: Why did the failure seem "obvious" to Arif bhai and Nazia?
qa.a: They felt confident judging the stall by what they know now, the heat and the dusty gate, without thinking about what Shreya's team knew in February.

qa.q: Which question from Shreya changed the review, and why?
qa.a: "When we chose biryani in February, what did we know?" It moved the talk from blame to the facts available then, like the evening timing and last year's sell-out.

qa.q: How might Shreya have felt hearing her family call the plan obviously wrong?
qa.a: She was already sore about the loss, so the easy blame probably stung, which is why she stopped to set the record straight.

grounding: At home, relatives call a failed fest stall obviously doomed, and a young woman asks what was actually known when the choice was made.

passage: Last monsoon our college trekking club cancelled a Sahyadri trek halfway because of a landslide warning, and twenty-two people had to be brought back in jeeps at extra cost. I'm Harish, the club secretary, and I sat in the review meeting the week after. Everyone went after Ojas, who had planned it. "Trekking in July? It was obviously risky." "He should have known." Ojas just stared at the table. I didn't think it was fair, but I didn't want a shouting match. So I pulled up the planning chat from June and read it out. The forecast then: light rain. The forest office had said the trail was open. Three other colleges had booked the same route. Then I asked, "Knowing only this, what would we have decided?" The room went quiet. Someone said, "Probably the same." We agreed next time to add a clear turn-back rule, not a scapegoat.

qa.q: How many people had to be brought back in jeeps?
qa.a: Twenty-two people.

qa.q: Why did the club members feel sure the trek was "obviously risky"?
qa.a: They knew the landslide warning had come and felt frustrated about the extra jeep costs, so July trekking looked reckless in hindsight. They forgot that the forecast and the forest office had said it was fine at the time.

qa.q: What did Harish choose to do instead of arguing, and why did it work?
qa.a: Harish read out the June planning chat and asked what they would have decided knowing only that. Seeing the old information made the blame fade.

qa.q: How might Ojas have felt while everyone blamed him?
qa.a: Ojas probably felt ashamed and alone, staring at the table, and may have been relieved when Harish showed the plan had been reasonable.

grounding: A club secretary sees a review blame the trek planner and brings back what was known then, turning blame into a fair lesson.

passage: I'm Arohi, the woman who runs the kitchen at a small café in Pune, and last spring I learned to write things down before they happen. Kamal, our young cook, pitched a South Indian breakfast menu. Before saying yes, I opened a notebook and wrote: "Forecast: 60% chance breakfast sales rise within two months. Reasons: office crowd, no dosa place nearby. Risks: road work planned somewhere in our area, dates unknown." Then we launched. Six weeks later, the metro work closed our lane, and breakfast sales fell. The owner came in angry. "Whose idea was this?" Kamal went pale. I opened the notebook and showed him the page. "We knew about road work but not when. The idea was sound; the timing was bad luck." The owner read it twice. "Fine. Keep the menu, and check again after the lane opens." Kamal made me extra filter coffee that evening.

qa.q: What chance of success did Arohi write in her forecast?
qa.a: 60% chance breakfast sales rise within two months.

qa.q: Why did Kamal go pale when the owner asked whose idea it was?
qa.a: Kamal was afraid of being blamed for the fall in sales, since the menu was Kamal's idea and the result looked bad.

qa.q: What choice did Arohi make before the launch that protected the team later?
qa.a: She wrote down her forecast, reasons and risks before launching. That record let the review separate the sound decision from the bad luck of the lane closure.

qa.q: How might the owner see the menu decision after reading the notebook?
qa.a: The owner seems to move from anger to fairness, seeing the risk had been noted and the timing was out of their hands, so the menu gets another chance.

grounding: A café lead writes her forecast and reasons before a menu launch, so when luck turns bad the review judges the process, not the cook.

passage:
Regional coordinator's note, community radio network. Written by Damini, after visiting the Aizawl station.
Lalremsiami, the station lead, is twenty-five and does something none of our other leads do. Before any big change, she writes a one-page note: what she expects, how sure she is, and why. In March she moved the farmers' show from morning to evening. Her note said: "65% chance more listeners; farmers told us mornings are busy. Risk: evening power cuts." The move failed; listeners dropped by a third. In the review, two volunteers blamed her. She took out the note. The power cuts had doubled that month because of line repairs, which nobody had predicted. The reasoning had been sound. The team agreed to try again after the repairs, and no one was blamed. I watched her keep calm and I want every station to use her one-page note. I've sent the template to all six leads.

qa.q: What time did Lalremsiami move the farmers' show to?
qa.a: From morning to evening.

qa.q: How do you think Lalremsiami felt when two volunteers blamed her, and what shows it?
qa.a: She may have felt stung, but she stayed calm and took out her note. Having written her reasons in advance let her face the review steadily.

qa.q: What did Damini decide to do after watching the review, and why?
qa.a: Damini sent Lalremsiami's one-page note template to all six station leads, so other reviews can separate good reasoning from bad luck.

qa.q: How might the two volunteers feel after seeing the note?
qa.a: They may feel a bit embarrassed for blaming Lalremsiami, but also reassured that their own future decisions will be judged fairly.

grounding: A coordinator's note describes a young station lead who writes forecasts and reasons before changes, so a failed move is not wrongly blamed on her.

passage: At the school canteen, Wasim, nine, bought a spicy paneer roll with his own twenty rupees. One bite and his eyes watered. He hated it. "Are you going to finish that?" asked Devika from his class, eating her plain idli. "I paid twenty rupees," Wasim said, and took another bite. His face turned red. He drank half his water bottle. He took another bite. "You don't even like it," Devika said. "But I paid." He chewed slowly, miserable, while the others ran out to play. By the last bite recess was almost over. Devika waited at the door. "You missed kho-kho," she said. Wasim wiped his eyes. "I didn't want to waste the money." "The money was already gone," Devika said. "You just wasted recess too."

qa.q: How much did Wasim pay for the paneer roll?
qa.a: Twenty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Wasim keep eating a roll he hated?
qa.a: He felt it would be a waste to stop because he had already paid, so he kept eating, miserable, even though the money was gone either way.

qa.q: What could Wasim do next time he buys something he doesn't like?
qa.a: He could stop after the first bites and ask himself what he wants to do now, like go and play, since eating more won't bring the twenty rupees back.

qa.q: How might Devika feel waiting at the door for Wasim?
qa.a: She probably felt a bit impatient and sorry for him, since he missed kho-kho for a roll he didn't even enjoy.

grounding: A boy keeps eating a spicy roll he hates because he paid for it, and misses recess games.

passage: I'm Leela. Last Sunday, visiting my friend Seema, I watched her son Tinku, ten, play a long property-trading board game with his cousins. The game had gone on for an hour and a half. The cousins had drifted off to the terrace. Tinku stayed, rolling for everyone, yawning. "Tinku, come play cricket," Seema called. "No, Mummy! I've been playing for ages. If I stop now, all that time is wasted." I can't say what he was thinking, but he kept going another half hour, sighing at every turn. By the time he packed it away, the cricket had ended. He sat on the steps, cross. Seema sat next to him and said softly, "The time was spent anyway, beta. The only question was what to do next."

qa.q: How long had the game gone on when the cousins gave up?
qa.a: The game had gone on for an hour and a half.

qa.q: Why might Tinku have kept playing a game he found boring?
qa.a: He seemed to feel that stopping would waste all the time already spent, so he kept going, bored and sighing, as if carrying on protected it.

qa.q: When Seema called him to cricket, what choice would have served Tinku better?
qa.a: He could have asked himself what he wanted to do now and gone to play cricket, since more board-game time wouldn't give back the hour and a half.

qa.q: How might Seema have felt watching Tinku sit alone with the game?
qa.a: Seema probably felt a mix of amusement and sympathy, and chose a gentle word afterward instead of a lecture.

grounding: A family friend watches a boy keep playing a boring board game alone because he has already spent so long on it.

subtype: Stuck in coaching or a course [Actor]
passage: I'm Jatin, and until last winter I spent four mornings a week at the swimming academy, from the age of eleven. By fifteen, a lanky boy, I hated it. The cold water at six, the chlorine in my eyes, the same laps. What I wanted was to join the school band and learn drums. But every time I thought of quitting, I thought of the four years and the fees Papa had paid in advance. It felt like throwing all that into the pool. So I kept going, grumpy, slower every month. One morning Ramesh sir, the coach, found me sitting on the edge, not getting in. "Jatin, if you were starting today, would you join this academy?" I said no before I could stop myself. He nodded. "Then the four years are already yours. They made you strong. Don't let them take the next four too." That week I talked to Papa.

qa.q: How many years had Jatin been at the swimming academy?
qa.a: Four years, since the age of eleven.

qa.q: Why did quitting feel like "throwing all that into the pool" to Jatin?
qa.a: Jatin felt torn: the years and the advance fees seemed to become wasted the moment he stopped, so continuing felt like protecting them, even though he hated it.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what choice did Jatin make afterwards?
qa.a: Ramesh sir's question about whether he would join today. Jatin's honest "no" led him to talk to Papa that week.

qa.q: How might Ramesh sir feel watching Jatin sit on the edge, not getting in?
qa.a: He likely felt concerned and sorry, seeing a strong swimmer who no longer wanted to be there, and cared more about Jatin's future than about keeping him.

grounding: A teenage boy stays at a swimming academy he hates because of the years and fees already spent, until his coach asks if he'd join today.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 11. Written by Himani, 3 September.
Pritam came to see me today, sent by his class teacher because he has looked exhausted for weeks. He told me he hates the computer science tuition he has attended for two years, three evenings a week. He says he would rather put that time into art, where he is doing well. When I asked why he continues, he said, "My mother, Sarita aunty, already paid for this year. And I've done two years. If I stop now, what was it for?" He said it looked like a reason, but he seemed trapped by it. I asked him what the next two years would look like if he kept going, and he went quiet. We made a plan: he will write down what he'd do with those three evenings, and I will meet him and his mother together next Tuesday.

qa.q: How many evenings a week does Pritam attend the computer science tuition?
qa.a: Three evenings a week.

qa.q: Why does Pritam keep going to tuition he hates?
qa.a: Pritam feels trapped, afraid the two years and this year's fees will be wasted if he stops. "What was it for?" shows the past feels like a debt to keep paying.

qa.q: What next step did Himani plan, and why could it help?
qa.a: Pritam will write down what he'd do with those evenings, and Himani will meet him with his mother next Tuesday. Looking forward and talking together can loosen the hold of the past fees.

qa.q: How might Sarita aunty feel about Pritam's tuition if she hears how exhausted he is?
qa.a: She may feel worried and perhaps surprised, since she may have thought the tuition was helping him, and may want to hear about the art.

grounding: A counsellor notes that a teenage boy keeps going to tuition he hates because of the fees and years already spent.

passage: Kashish, you keep saying you can't break up because you've been together three years. Let your Avni masi tell you something. When I was twenty, in Indore, I had a boyfriend from my college. For the first year it was lovely. By the third year, we barely talked. He'd cancel plans, I'd cry, we'd make up, same thing again. My friends asked why I stayed. I said, "Three years! I can't just throw that away." It felt like leaving would make all those years a mistake. So I stayed one more year. Then one day, sitting alone in a café where he didn't show up again, I thought: the three years happened. They're mine. Staying won't make them better. It only takes the fourth. I ended it the next week. It hurt. But masi was free by twenty-one. So think about the next year, beta, not only the last three.

qa.q: How old was Avni masi when she ended the relationship?
qa.a: Masi was free by twenty-one.

qa.q: Why did young Avni stay in the relationship even after it stopped working?
qa.a: Leaving felt like it would turn three years into a mistake, so staying seemed to protect the past, even though it cost her more time.

qa.q: What was Avni's turning point, and what did she decide?
qa.a: Sitting alone in the café when he didn't show up, she realised the past years were already hers and staying only takes more. She ended it the next week.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel hearing this story from Avni masi?
qa.a: Kashish may feel understood and less guilty about wanting to leave, and may start thinking about the next year instead of the last three.

grounding: An aunt tells Kashish how she once stayed in a failing relationship because leaving felt like wasting the years already spent.

passage: The transfer window at the university office closed at four, and at 3:10 the queue still stretched down the corridor. Ankita held two forms: one to stay in third-year architecture, one to switch to the psychology course she'd been sneaking into for months. Her friend Francis stood beside her, holding her bag. "You've filled both," he said. "Which one?" "I should stay. Two whole years. All those models, those nights. If I leave, it's all for nothing." "Do you like architecture?" She looked at the floor. "Not since first year." The queue shuffled forward. 3:35. "If you were starting today," Francis said, "which form would you pick?" Ankita didn't answer for a while. "Psychology," she whispered. "The two years still taught you things. They're not nothing." At 3:52 she reached the window and handed over the psychology form, her hands shaking.

qa.q: What time did the transfer window close?
qa.a: At four.

qa.q: Why does Ankita feel she should stay in architecture?
qa.a: The two years of models and late nights feel like they would become worthless if she left. Staying feels like a way to honour that effort.

qa.q: What question helped Ankita choose, and why did it work under time pressure?
qa.a: "If you were starting today, which form would you pick?" It cut through the past and made her face what she wants now, so she handed in the psychology form.

qa.q: How might Francis feel as he watches Ankita hand in the form?
qa.a: He is probably relieved and proud of her, while understanding why her hands are shaking. 🙂

grounding: A student almost stays in a degree she no longer likes because of the years spent, and switches just before the deadline.

passage:
March. Uday, twenty-four, sat in the flying school's canteen in Baramati, staring at his logbook. His parents had sold a plot of land to pay the fees. Papa told every relative, "My son will be a pilot." Uday felt sick before every lesson. He didn't want to fly. But how could he say so after all that money?
April. His sister Harsha came to visit. She found him awake at 2 a.m. "Tell me honestly." He did. She listened. "Papa's pride is his to handle," she said gently. "Your life is yours. Let's talk to them together."
May. At home, on the swing in the courtyard, Uday told his parents, with Harsha beside him. Papa said nothing for a long time. Amma cried. Then Papa said, "The land is gone either way, son. I don't want to lose you too." They began talking about what Uday actually wanted.

qa.q: What did Uday's parents sell to pay the fees?
qa.a: They had sold a plot of land.

qa.q: Why did Uday feel he couldn't tell his parents he didn't want to fly?
qa.a: They had spent so much money and Papa had told every relative, so quitting felt like wasting their sacrifice and hurting their pride.

qa.q: Which choice made the honest conversation possible?
qa.a: Telling Harsha the truth and agreeing to talk to his parents together. Having her beside him made it easier to be kind and honest.

qa.q: How might Papa feel when he says "I don't want to lose you too"?
qa.a: He is sad about the land and his hopes, but he cares more about his son's happiness than about the money already spent. 🤍

grounding: A young man feels trapped in flying school because his parents sold land and told everyone, until his sister helps him talk honestly.

passage: Ritu, you asked why your Kalyani aunty came back from Australia so suddenly all those years ago. I'll tell you. I was twenty-five. My parents had spent their savings and taken a loan for my nursing diploma in Melbourne. Appa told the whole street. When I realised it wasn't the life I wanted, I felt I couldn't come back. Every phone call, Amma would say, "We gave everything for this." She meant it lovingly, but each time it felt like a chain. I stayed six more months, miserable. Then one night, on a crackling call, I said, "Amma, Appa, I'm grateful. And I'm not happy. The money's spent whether I stay or not. Can we talk about what's best from now?" There was silence. Then Appa said, "Come home, kanna." It wasn't easy after that. But it was honest. That's what I want you to know.

qa.q: Where did Kalyani go for her nursing diploma?
qa.a: In Melbourne.

qa.q: Why did Amma's words "We gave everything for this" feel like a chain to Kalyani?
qa.a: Her parents' spending and pride made continuing feel like a duty, so leaving felt like betraying their sacrifice, even though she was unhappy.

qa.q: What did Kalyani choose to say on the phone, and why did it work?
qa.a: She thanked her parents, told them honestly she was unhappy, and asked to talk about what was best from now. Being both kind and honest let them listen.

qa.q: How might Kalyani's parents have felt during the silence on the call?
qa.a: They likely felt shock and sadness about their sacrifice, mixed with love, which is why Appa ended the silence with "Come home, kanna."

grounding: An aunt recalls feeling trapped abroad by her parents' spending and pride, and having a kind, honest conversation with them.

passage: Behind her house in a village near Dharwad, Malti had spent two years and most of her savings on a mushroom shed. Her brother Hrithik had helped build it, and her friend Pankaj from the agriculture office had brought the spawn. But every summer the humidity went wrong and the crop rotted. This July, standing in the stink of another failed batch, Malti asked herself a question Pankaj had once asked her: "If you had never built this shed, would you start it today, knowing what you know?" She sat on an upturned bucket for a long time. The answer was no. She cried a little, for the money, the early mornings, the hope. Then she wrote down what she'd learned: check water, check buyers first, start small. The next week she and Hrithik turned the shed into a shelter for her goats. "Not a waste," Hrithik said. "It's a good roof."

qa.q: How long had Malti spent on the mushroom shed?
qa.a: Two years and most of her savings.

qa.q: Why did Malti cry after deciding to stop?
qa.a: She was grieving the money, the early mornings and the hope she had put in. Stopping was right, but the loss still hurt.

qa.q: What question helped Malti decide, and what did she do after answering it?
qa.a: Whether she would start the shed today, knowing what she knows now. When the answer was no, she wrote down her lessons and turned the shed into a goat shelter.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see the end of the mushroom project?
qa.a: He seems to see it without shame, calling the shed "a good roof," which helps Malti feel the effort wasn't wasted.

grounding: A young woman in a village asks if she would start her failing mushroom shed today, grieves the cost, learns from it and moves on.

passage: In Accra, Rania had spent two years and almost all her savings turning an old van into a food truck. The city had refused her licence twice because the van was too old for the new rules. Her friend Kwame found her sitting on the van's step, the permit letter in her lap. "Appeal again?" he asked. "I was going to," she said. "I've put so much into it. I can't just stop." Then she paused. "Kwame, if I'd never bought this van, would I buy it today?" "Knowing what you know now?" "No," she admitted. "Never." She was quiet for a while, and her eyes filled. "Two years." "Two years you learned to cook for crowds and run a business," Kwame said. The next month she sold the van for parts and rented a small stall in the market. She pinned the old permit letter above the counter.

qa.q: How many times had the city refused Rania's licence?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: Why was Rania about to appeal again?
qa.a: Rania was afraid of losing two years and almost all her savings, so stopping felt like losing everything. Continuing seemed to protect what she had spent.

qa.q: What question changed Rania's decision, and how did she move forward?
qa.a: She asked whether she would buy the van today, knowing what she knows now. When the answer was no, she sold it for parts and rented a market stall, taking what she had learned.

qa.q: What might Kwame be feeling as Rania's eyes fill with tears?
qa.a: Kwame is likely sad for Rania but also hopeful, wanting the two years seen as learning, not failure.

grounding: A young woman abroad asks if she would buy her food-truck van today, grieves the loss, and moves on to a market stall.

passage:
Friday
Dear Diary,
At recess I played marbles with Shankar. I won his green cat's-eye marble! I said "yes!" and put it in my pocket. Then I kept playing. Then I lost my red one. My red one! The one Nana gave me. I cried so hard that Miss asked if I was hurt. I wasn't. I just felt terrible. Shankar said, "But you won the green one, so it's the same." It's NOT the same. The green one felt nice for a minute. Losing the red one felt bad for the whole day. I don't even know why. Mummy hugged me. "My poor boy. Losing feels bigger than winning, na?" Tomorrow I will ask Shankar if we can swap back. I'll give him his green one.
Madhav

qa.q: Who gave Madhav the red marble?
qa.a: Nana gave it to him.

qa.q: Why did losing the red marble feel worse to Madhav than winning the green one felt good?
qa.a: The red marble was his, and giving up something he owned felt much heavier than getting a new one, even though it was a fair swap. It also came from Nana.

qa.q: What does Madhav plan to do tomorrow, and why might it help?
qa.a: He plans to ask Shankar to swap back. Getting the red marble back would ease the loss, and it shows he can find a fair fix instead of staying upset.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel about Madhav crying so much after the game?
qa.a: Shankar may feel confused, since to Shankar one marble for one marble is fair, and maybe a bit worried he did something wrong.

grounding: A boy writes in his diary that losing his marble made him cry harder than winning a marble made him happy.

passage: On Uttarayan morning in their village near Anand, Tushar, eight, stood on the roof with his sister Ganga and a stack of kites. By noon he had cut two kites from the neighbour's roof. Each time he shouted "Kaypo che!", danced a moment, and flew on. At two, a purple kite crossed his string, and snap, his favourite yellow kite drifted away over the fields. Tushar burst out crying. He sat by the water tank and wouldn't get up. "You cut two of theirs!" Ganga said. "That's two to one!" "That was mine," he sobbed. "The yellow one." Ganga sat beside him and gave him a sesame laddoo. "Losing yours feels bigger, na?" He nodded. After a while he picked up a red kite. "Tie it for me, didi?"

qa.q: How many kites had Tushar cut by noon?
qa.a: He had cut two kites from the neighbour's roof.

qa.q: Why did Tushar cry so much about his yellow kite when he had just won two?
qa.a: Losing his own favourite kite felt heavier than cutting two of theirs felt good. Something he owned mattered more to him than an equal gain.

qa.q: What helped Tushar get back to flying?
qa.a: Ganga sat with him, gave him a laddoo and named how losing feels bigger, instead of arguing that two beats one. Feeling understood let him pick up a new kite.

qa.q: If you were Ganga, why might Tushar's tears surprise you?
qa.a: You'd see that he was winning, two to one, so the tears seem out of proportion, until you notice how much the lost kite belonged to him.

grounding: On a kite-flying festival, a boy cries far harder over losing his kite than he celebrated cutting two others.

subtype: Fear of losing rank or friends [Actor]
passage: At the city sports complex, Neel, fifteen, was the best badminton player in the under-16 group. Everyone at Court 2 knew it. When coach Kalyani ma'am announced a new squash programme, she looked at him. "You'd be good. Same footwork." Ritu, from his batch, signed up immediately. "Come on, Neel, it'll be fun." Neel shook his head. "I'm happy here." But he kept glancing at the glass squash court during breaks. He imagined walking in and losing to kids younger than him. Everyone watching the badminton star miss the ball. That picture made his stomach clench. At Court 2, he was number one. On the squash court, he'd be nobody. Two months later, Ritu was playing a friendly match on the squash court, laughing. Neel watched through the glass. He still won every badminton game. But the complex felt smaller somehow.

qa.q: Which group was Neel the best badminton player in?
qa.a: The under-16 group.

qa.q: Why did Neel refuse to try squash even though he kept glancing at the court?
qa.a: Losing his place as the badminton star felt worse than any fun or skill he might gain. The picture of missing the ball in front of others made his stomach clench.

qa.q: What small step could Neel take to try squash without risking his standing all at once?
qa.a: He could ask Kalyani ma'am for a private practice session or play with Ritu when the court is quiet, so he can be a beginner without an audience.

qa.q: How might Ritu see Neel's choice to stay only with badminton?
qa.a: Ritu might feel a bit disappointed at not sharing the new sport with Neel, and may wonder why someone so good is afraid to try.

grounding: A teenage boy refuses to try squash because losing his status as the best badminton player feels worse than any gain.

subtype: Fear of losing rank or friends [Actor]
passage:
Dear Anand,
Remember I told you about the new kids from the drama group who asked me to sit with them at lunch? I didn't go. I've been with the same four guys since Class 5. We're known as the cricket lot. I'm not even the best player, just the boy who keeps score, but I've got a spot. If I start hanging out with the drama people and it doesn't work out, I might lose my place with the cricket lot and end up with nobody. That scares me more than anything.
But here's the thing. The drama group is making a short film, and they asked me to help with the music. You know I've always wanted to try that. I said I was busy. I wasn't.
Sometimes I feel my world is the size of one lunch table.
What would you do?
Your cousin,
Tarun

qa.q: Since which class has Tarun been with the same four guys?
qa.a: Since Class 5.

qa.q: Why did Tarun say he was busy when the drama group asked him to help with the music?
qa.a: He fears that trying the new group might cost him his place with the cricket lot and leave him with nobody. That possible loss feels bigger than the chance to do music he has always wanted.

qa.q: What small choice could Tarun make to test his fear without giving anything up?
qa.a: He could help with the film's music for one afternoon while still sitting with the cricket lot at lunch, and see whether he really loses anything.

qa.q: If you were Anand reading this letter, what might you want to tell Tarun?
qa.a: You might want to reassure him that real friends won't drop him for trying music, and encourage him to say yes to the film.

grounding: A teenage boy writes to his cousin that fear of losing his place in his friend group keeps him from joining a drama group's film.
